input:
Over the course of one summer month, the performance of a natural-draft cooling tower located at a chemical site was carefully logged. During this period, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 27 °C. The approach, which is essentially the difference between the temperature of the water leaving the tower and the wet-bulb temperature, came to 4 K, which means that the leaving water temperature was 31 °C. The range, which describes the fall in water temperature as the water passes through the tower, was 5 K, so the entering water temperature was 36 °C.

It is worth noting that a natural-draft tower has no fan: instead, air is drawn through the fill purely by buoyancy, because the air inside the tower becomes warmer, more humid and therefore less dense than the air outside, and the considerable height of the tower turns this density difference into a driving pressure. As a result, the performance of the tower is closely tied to the weather, and in particular to the wet-bulb temperature of the ambient air. The approach shows how close the tower came to the wet-bulb limit, while the range shows how much cooling each unit of circulating water received during the month that was actually observed.

Importantly, performance outside the logged month was not measured at all. In winter, when wet-bulb temperatures are much lower, the driving force, the air flow and the water-side behaviour would all be different, and icing at the air inlet could become an issue, so the summer figures should not be extrapolated to winter conditions or treated as a year-round characterisation of the tower.
target:
Performance of a natural-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. The mean wet-bulb temperature over the month was 27 °C. The approach, the difference between the leaving water temperature and the wet-bulb temperature, was 4 K, and the leaving water temperature was therefore 31 °C. The range, the fall in water temperature across the tower, was 5 K, and the entering water temperature was 36 °C.

A natural-draft tower has no fan. Air moves through the fill because the air inside the tower, warmed and humidified by the water, is less dense than the air outside, and the height of the tower converts that density difference into a driving pressure. The air flow the tower can draw is set by the weather and by the heat load together, and the water temperatures the tower reaches follow the wet-bulb temperature of the entering air. The approach is the margin the tower holds above that limit: no cooling tower can cool water below the wet-bulb temperature, and the approach states how close the leaving water came to it during the logged month. The range states the cooling done to each unit of water circulated, and with the circulation rate it fixes the heat the tower rejected.

The logged month is a summer month, and the record describes summer operation. Performance outside the logged month was not measured. At winter wet-bulb temperatures the driving force, the air flow and the water-side behaviour all change, and the tower may also face icing at the air inlet, a condition the summer record does not cover. No winter approach or range is stated, and none is inferred from the summer figures. The record supports statements about the tower at the wet-bulb temperatures and loadings of the logged month; a design or guarantee figure for the year would need measurements across the seasons the tower is required to serve.
